video_title: The Kansas City Fed President on the First Jackson Hole of the Warsh Era | Odd Lots
gist: Kansas City Fed President Jeff Schmid, interviewed by Tracy Alloway and Joe Weisenthal at the 49th Jackson Hole symposium (theme: financial innovation in payments), says policy is still 'fairly accommodative,' that inflation in the mid-3s 'has to be addressed' while the labor market is fine, and that r* is likely settling at a structurally higher base than pre-2008. He frames higher long yields as the product of commercial-versus-public competition for credit driven partly by the AI/data-center build, and aligns himself with new Chairman Kevin Warsh's push for open FOMC debate — while noting Warsh's new task forces have not yet engaged the regional presidents.

themes.theme: Hawkish tilt: inflation unfinished, policy still accommodative

insights.claim: The Kansas City Fed president believes the labor market is in good shape while inflation work remains undone, an explicit asymmetry that argues against near-term easing.
insights.speaker: Jeff Schmid (Kansas City Fed President)
insights.so_what: A regional Fed president publicly weighting inflation over employment is a hawkish data point for pricing the path of the funds rate and front-end duration.
insights.quote: I think the labor force is in a pretty good place. We haven't done our job yet on inflation.

insights.claim: A sitting Fed president characterizes the current stance of rates as 'fairly accommodative,' implying he sees room for policy to be tighter rather than looser despite an economy he describes as growing well.
insights.speaker: Jeff Schmid
insights.so_what: If more of the committee shares this read, market pricing for cuts is too aggressive; watch for hawkish dissents at coming meetings.
insights.quote: I think from my standpoint personally, I think we're at a fairly accommodative place for rates right now.

insights.claim: Inflation has surged back into the mid-3% range and a Fed official says addressing it is non-negotiable because it is one of the two statutory mandates.
insights.speaker: Jeff Schmid
insights.so_what: Confirms inflation is running roughly 150bp above target from the Fed's own mouth — relevant to breakevens and real-rate positioning.
insights.quote: we clearly have had a bit of a surge into the mid threes. Uh, it has to be addressed.

insights.claim: The last mile from 3% to 2% inflation is described as the hardest part of the journey because the committee starts fearing overshoot and mistimes decisions in either direction.
insights.speaker: Jeff Schmid
insights.so_what: Suggests policy error risk is two-sided and elevated near the target — a case for volatility in front-end rates rather than a smooth glide path.

insights.claim: Unemployment has fallen from 4.3% to 4.1% over the prior year, and a Fed president says he is optimistic about the durability of the expansion.
insights.speaker: Jeff Schmid
insights.so_what: A falling unemployment rate removes the labor-market excuse for cuts and reinforces the hawkish inflation focus.

insights.claim: A Fed president argues the neutral rate is normalizing but at a higher base level than prevailed even before 2008, meaning today's rates are less restrictive than they look.
insights.speaker: Jeff Schmid
insights.so_what: A higher r* re-rates the entire term structure: it caps how far the Fed can cut and argues for structurally higher long-run yields.

insights.claim: The yield curve is described as fairly normalized for an economy growing between 2% and 3.5%, implying current long-end levels are seen as fundamentally justified rather than a market dislocation.
insights.speaker: Jeff Schmid
insights.so_what: A Fed official validating high long yields as 'normal' reduces the odds of intervention to suppress them; fade bets on official long-end support.
insights.quote: it seems to me like the demand or the, uh, the yield curve is fairly normalized inside of an economy that's growing somewhere between 2 and 3.5%

themes.theme: Long-end yields as a credit supply-and-demand story

insights.claim: Higher long-term yields are framed as the price outcome of commercial borrowers competing with government borrowing for a finite pool of credit, not as a pure inflation-premium story.
insights.speaker: Jeff Schmid
insights.so_what: If crowding-out is the driver, long yields stay high while both Treasury issuance and corporate capex demand run hot — a headwind for duration regardless of Fed cuts.
insights.quote: If there's more demand for credit, uh, you're going to have a competition between commercial and public credit

insights.claim: The Fed retains some influence over long rates through balance sheet duration actions even though its policy tools target the short end, as it demonstrated post-2008 and post-2020.
insights.speaker: Jeff Schmid
insights.so_what: Keeps balance-sheet composition (not just the funds rate) live as a policy lever if the 30-year keeps rising — a tail scenario worth pricing.
insights.quote: we did take some actions inside of our balance sheet to pull duration into the into our balance sheet, which did influence some of the longer rates

insights.claim: The tightening effect of higher long yields is partly behavioral and can be overwhelmed when projected returns are high enough — an 80 basis point move in the ten-year may not change a business model at all.
insights.speaker: Jeff Schmid
insights.so_what: Undercuts the 'bond yields do the Fed's work for it' thesis — if AI-era project returns are high, higher yields won't slow investment and the Fed may need to act itself.
insights.quote: you might think that the returns on that are so astronomical that a, that a 80 basis point move in the ten year isn't going to affect your your business model

insights.claim: Rate hikes almost never kill a factory decision because long-lived capex is priced off the ten-year, but they do bite immediately on current-asset decisions like whether to pre-buy inventory on a line of credit.
insights.speaker: Jeff Schmid
insights.so_what: Points to inventory and working-capital cycles — not fixed investment — as the transmission channel to watch when policy rates move; relevant to distributors, wholesalers and bank C&I loan growth.
insights.quote: I'm going to pay another 25 or 50 basis points on my line of credit, maybe I maybe I stall that decision

themes.theme: AI/data-center boom and commodity crowding out

insights.claim: A Fed president identifies the data center and AI build as the most dynamic growth component inside GDP and says the Fed needs to isolate how much of the growth number is cyclical to this boom.
insights.speaker: Jeff Schmid
insights.so_what: If the Fed concludes AI capex is a transitory flywheel rather than trend growth, it changes the read on both potential output and how much tightening is needed.
insights.quote: that's why we got to peel the onion back and try to figure out what parts of the growth onion are being driven specifically by this kind of boom effect

insights.claim: Data center construction is competing directly for steel, copper and machinery inputs used by other industries, and a Fed president calls untangling that a really important part of getting inflation back to 2%.
insights.speaker: Jeff Schmid
insights.so_what: Frames AI capex as an inflationary force via industrial commodities — bullish for copper/steel demand, and a reason Fed officials may stay hawkish longer.

themes.theme: Payments innovation: atomic settlement, duration and liquidity

insights.claim: The Federal Reserve moves $5 to $10 trillion a day across multiple payment rails, and its explicit goal is to make payments boring.
insights.speaker: Jeff Schmid
insights.so_what: Scale framing for anyone sizing the payments-infrastructure opportunity and the systemic stakes of settlement changes.
insights.quote: we move 5 to $10 trillion a day through the system, through multiple different pipes, payment pipes.

insights.claim: The move to atomic settlement — instant transfer and instant reconciliation that eliminates float — is coming and will be both innovative and disruptive to existing intermediaries.
insights.speaker: Jeff Schmid
insights.so_what: Float income and settlement-lag business models are the losers; watch banks, card networks and clearing intermediaries whose revenue depends on payment friction.
insights.quote: we're moving toward I've seen the words atomic settlement, uh, in the marketplace, which is actually when payments are actually going to be instant

insights.claim: Instant settlement forces pre-proven liquidity behind every payment, which is why the Fed's two dominant future preoccupations will be asset duration and liquidity.
insights.speaker: Jeff Schmid
insights.so_what: Signals the direction of future bank regulation and reserve demand: instant settlement raises structural demand for HQLA and reserves, with implications for repo and bank funding costs.
insights.quote: we're going to be talking a lot more as we go forward about two main things in our world. One is duration, duration of assets. The second is going to be liquidity.

themes.theme: Labor force structural shift and the boomer retirement wave

insights.claim: Baby boomers are retiring at roughly 4 million people per year and a Fed president expects this labor force turnover to continue for about another decade, ultimately as a net positive for the economy.
insights.speaker: Jeff Schmid
insights.so_what: A shrinking-supply labor market means a low unemployment print may not signal a hot economy — it changes how much slack the Fed thinks it needs to create.
insights.quote: people in my generation, the baby boomers, I mean, we're retiring at about 4 million people per year

insights.claim: A Fed president says retirement letter volume in the last three months exceeded the prior three years and frames the resulting loss of institutional knowledge as a risk to be solved by using AI to transfer expertise from retirees to younger staff.
insights.speaker: Jeff Schmid
insights.so_what: Real-world adoption case for enterprise AI: institutional knowledge capture driven by demographics, a durable demand source independent of the hype cycle.
insights.quote: I worry about the intellectual muscle that we're losing in that

themes.theme: The Warsh Fed: dissent, communication and unengaged task forces

insights.claim: A dissent at the FOMC is best read not as disagreement about the data but as a statement that the risks between the inflation and employment mandates are weighted differently than the majority believes.
insights.speaker: Jeff Schmid
insights.so_what: A cleaner way to read dissents in statements: they map the committee's risk-weighting distribution, which is more predictive of the rate path than headline vote counts.
insights.quote: the dissent is really a mechanism of saying, I think the risks, uh, between those two mandates are weighted differently than you think they are.

insights.claim: The new Fed chair's stated preference is for the central bank to be on page B12 rather than A1 — a deliberate reduction in the Fed's communicative prominence and a move away from forward guidance.
insights.speaker: Jeff Schmid
insights.so_what: Less forward guidance means less pre-positioned markets and more repricing around actual decisions — structurally higher rates volatility around FOMC dates.
insights.quote: better the fed be on the page B 12 versus A1

insights.claim: The new chair's emphasis is on open internal debate and multiple thoughtful dissents rather than consensus enforcement, which a regional president explicitly endorses over a 'my way or the highway' style.
insights.speaker: Jeff Schmid
insights.so_what: Expect more visible dissents and a less unified message from the FOMC, making individual speakers more market-moving than under a consensus-driven chair.

insights.claim: The 15 people named to the new Fed chair's task forces have not yet been in real dialogue with regional Fed presidents, with engagement expected only once their research emerges.
insights.speaker: Jeff Schmid
insights.so_what: Means any Fed reform on data measurement or communications is still upstream of the FOMC — timeline for actual framework change is later than headlines suggest.
insights.quote: But as of now, not really.

insights.claim: The Fed's own communications should avoid making markets fragile, with the priority being to preserve the market's function of pricing risk rather than to substitute official guidance for it.
insights.speaker: Jeff Schmid
insights.so_what: Signals reduced willingness to backstop or steer asset prices verbally — a subtle removal of the perceived Fed put.
insights.quote: more important that the market has a function to decide risk and price. And you want to make sure that market is strong and that you're not making it in any way fragile with some of your communications.

insights.claim: Asked whether a smaller deficit would make hitting the inflation target easier, the Kansas City Fed president declined to engage and reframed the Fed's job purely as reacting to the data produced by fiscal and legislative decisions.
insights.speaker: Jeff Schmid
insights.so_what: Confirms no fiscal offset is coming from the Fed's side — the term premium from deficits gets absorbed by markets, not neutralized by policy.

insights.claim: Even after the interview, the hosts conclude the new chair's reaction function remains ambiguous, with the central unanswered question being whether the Fed will actually raise rates given inflation above 3%.
insights.speaker: Joe Weisenthal
insights.so_what: The live tail risk in rates markets is a hike, not just fewer cuts — worth checking whether options pricing reflects that possibility.
insights.quote: I still think there is some ambiguity about the reaction function of the new sort of Kevin Warsh approach
